Rapid microwave-assisted pretreatment using a ternary deep eutectic solvent for lignin fractionation of eucalyptus
<::logo: Unknown Check for updates A red and yellow banner-like symbol is centered within a blue circle, all on a light gray square button.::>
Zhuang Liuᵃ, Yi Houᵃ, Songqing Huᵇ,*

a State Key Laboratory of Pulp and Paper Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou 510640, PR China b School of Food Science and Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou 510640, PR China
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: DES Microwave Pretreatment Delignification

ABSTRACT This work developed a strategy for rapid microwave-assisted refining of eucalyptus wood in 30 min using a ternary DES (lactic acid: choline chloride: polyethylene glycol 400, 10:1 + 5%) with an excellent delignification rate of 89.73%. The test of Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs shows that the acidity and polarity of the solution greatly influence the delignification rate. The polyethylene glycol 400 increased the solubility of lignin in the solvent, improved the delignification rate, and protected cellulose from degradation. The gel permeation chromatography, 2D-HSQC NMR, and ³¹P NMR analysis show that the lignin obtained after DES treatment had low molecular weight, small polydispersity index, and relatively rich content of β-O-4 and phenolic hydroxyl groups, which has great application potential in high-value-added products from lignin. At the same time, the main products of the simulated reaction of the lignin model compound were monophenols and Hibbert ketone, and the possible reaction mechanism of changes in lignin during treatment was given. Our study lays a foundation for applying DES in biomass refining and the high-value utilization of lignin.

# 1. Introduction The depletion of fossil fuels and pressing environmental concerns have engendered a significant inclination toward the pursuit of sustainable and renewable resources. Lignocellulosic biomass, characterized by its abundance and renewability, holds significant potential as a viable substitute for fossil-based feedstock. This biomass can be effectively transformed into both fuels and chemicals, offering a promising avenue for sustainable energy production and resource utilization (Liu et al., 2019; Rana et al., 2022, 2023; Rana, 2022). The primary constituents of lignocellulose are cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Lignin is the wealthiest resource of aromatic compounds in nature, and there are various applications for the utilization of this substance in the production of high-value fine chemicals, fuel products, and functional materials (Shen et al., 2019a). However, removing lignin from lignocellulosic biomass is difficult due to its complicated internal network structure and stubborn lignin.

To overcome the inherent stubbornness of lignocellulose, researchers have developed different pretreatment methods to upgrade lignocellu- lose biomass into high-value products (Haghighi Mood et al., 2013). However, the strong corrosive nature of diluted acid, the high energy

and high-pressure requirements of steam explosion and hydrothermal pretreatment, the high volatility of organic solvents used in organic solvent pretreatment, and the high cost, toxicity, and poor biodegrad- ability of ionic liquids are some drawbacks that are typically associated with these techniques (Ci et al., 2020).

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), eutectic mixtures with a lower eutectic temperature than the ideal liquid combination, have recently received much interest in biomass pretreatment due to their remarkable selectivity for lignin removal (Tan et al., 2018; Alvarez-Vasco et al., 2016; da Costa Lopes et al., 2020). The DES system comprises a minimum of two hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) (Smith et al., 2014). Due to its cheap cost, non-toxicity, biodegradability, and economical production, the quaternary ammonium salt is the most extensively used HBA for DES, specifically choline chloride (ChCl) (Schutyser et al., 2018). ChCl-based DESs have been extensively utilized in diverse fields as an eco-friendly solvent alternative (Smith et al., 2014; Maugeri and de Maria, 2012; Zafarani-Moattar et al., 2016). However, the study of DES pretreatment usually focuses on non-wood (more than 80%) (Zhou et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2020; Wang and Lee, 2021). A more comprehensive investigation could be conducted regarding the availability of raw wood resources,

especially focusing on eucalyptus, which is widely cultivated as hard-wood and exhibits a significant rate of production (Shen et al., 2019a). Compared with non-wood biomass materials, the dense structure of hardwood is more difficult to deconstruct. Therefore, it usually takes 6–12 h or more to get relatively satisfactory pretreatment results in the few studies on DES pretreatment of eucalyptus (Hong et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2019b; Chen et al., 2021; Soares et al., 2021). Long pretreatment time and the acidity of DES will lead to lignin condensation and reduce the efficiency of enzyme treatment (Hong et al., 2020a). In addition, long-term pretreatment will lead to various side effects and degradation of DES and cellulose (Morais et al., 2021). Hence, it is imperative to expeditiously execute the delignification process to segregate biomass into superior-grade cellulose fibers and lignin. Microwave pretreatment has been widely employed in many bio-refining processes due to its non-contact heat source, low residence time, and minimal adverse ef-fects (Zhong et al., 2022; Muley et al., 2019). Furthermore, microwave radiation has been demonstrated to improve the ionic properties of DES and raise the molecular polarity (Chen and Wan, 2018). Microwave-assisted deep eutectic solvents (DES) have been proven effective for delignification of non-wood biomass feedstocks. For instance, Yan et al. (2023) treated rice straw continuously for 4 min under microwave irradiation (680 W) at a 1:30 solid to liquid ratio using a ternary DES (choline chloride: oxalic acid: lactic acid 1:0.5:1, molar ratio), yielding a 63.4% lignin removal rate. Chourasia et al (Chourasia et al., 2022). employed a choline chloride/ethylene glycol/NiCl2·6H2O system (molar ratio 1:2:0.016 with 20 wt% water as co-solvent) to treat sugarcane bagasse at 100°C for 30 min at 10% solid loading, reaching 84% delignification. Ji et al (Ji et al., 2020). utilized a ternary DES (ChCl-Gly-Al at molar ratio 1:2:0.2) under consecutive ultrasound (20 + 28 + 40 kHz, room temperature, 30 min) and microwave (80°C, 20 min) treatment of garlic skin to attain 90.14% lignin removal. Hence, it is plausible that the utilization of microwaves can reduce the duration of the reaction process in DES pretreatment of eucalyptus compared with DES pretreatment alone and achieve similar or even higher efficiency.

This study has devised an eco-friendly, gentle, and effective tech- nique for pretreatment by utilizing a ternary deep eutectic solvent to fractionate lignin from eucalyptus. Furthermore, the potential deligni- fication mechanism was elucidated through an investigation of the structural modifications of lignin pre- and post-treatment, as well as the simulation of the reaction process utilizing lignin model compounds.

2. Experimental materials and methods

## 2.1. Materials Samples of Eucalyptus were obtained from a commercial forest farm in Paiyang Mountain, China. The composition of the Eucalyptus was determined to be 25.68% lignin, 46.40% cellulose, and 27.92% hemi-cellulose, based on the dried extracted raw materials. The specific experimental procedures and relevant formulas could be found in the supply materials (Note. S2). Eucalyptus wood powder passing through 40 mesh sieves was selected as the raw material (RM). The milled wood lignin (MWL) and alkali lignin (AL) were obtained based on the reported routes (Wen et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023). The support information could include specific steps (Note. S1). The reagents used in this work are analytically pure and purchased from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd.

## 2.2. Methods ### 2.2.1. Preparation of DESs Several commonly used DESs for biomass pretreatments were prepared. Specific components and proportions can be found in Tab. S1. Specifically, a beaker was filled with a specified molar ratio of HBAs and HBDs. The obtained DESs were then kept at room temperature after being agitated in a water bath at 60°C to produce a clear solvent.

### 2.2.2. DES pretreatment and DES recycling The pretreatment process was conducted utilizing a conical flask, wherein the biomass concentration was maintained at 10 wt% (5.00 g of dry biomass and 50.00 g of reagents). The pretreatment was carried out under different target conditions (solvent type, heating mode, time, etc.) The resulting liquid and solid were transferred to a 500 mL beaker containing 250 mL of washing solvent (acetone: ethanol 1:1 v:v) and agitated for 6 h after pretreatment. Following that, the combined solution was filtered through a G2 glass filter, and the solid residue (SR) was washed with washing solvent until the filtrate was colorless. Rotary evaporation was used to concentrate the filtrate, which was subsequently placed into water to precipitate lignin. The SR and lignin obtained from the DES pretreatment (DESL) were dried in a vacuum oven at 40°C. By evaporating the liquid, DES was recovered and reused.

2.2.3. Component analysis of SR The lignin content in SR was determined by the two-step acid hy- drolysis (Shen et al., 2019b), the cellulose content in SR was determined by the nitric acid-alcohol method, and hemicellulose content was calculated by subtraction. The specific experimental procedures and relevant formulas could be found in the supply materials (Note. S2).

2.2.4. Measurement of the Kamlet–Taft (K-T) solvatochromic parameters of DESs The K-T solvatochromic parameters of DESs used in this work were measured based on reported routes (Dwamena and Raynie, 2020), where α stands for hydrogen bond acidity, the β stands for hydrogen bond alkalinity, and the π* stands for the polarity of the solvent. The specific steps and relevant formulas can be found in the support information (Note. S3).

2.2.5. Characterizations of lignin The application of gel permeation chromatography (GPC) was employed to assess the acetylation of materials for the purpose of determining the distribution of molecular weight (Mw) in lignin. The chemical structures of lignin were studied using Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy and 2D-HSQC NMR. The 31P NMR spectra were used to measure the phenolic hydroxyl, alcohol hydroxyl, and carboxyl concentrations of lignin. The specific steps and relevant for- mulas can be found in the support information (Note. S4).

Analysis of simulated reactions by model compound The simulation reaction of lignin in the solvent system was carried out with the typical model compound Guaiacylglycerol-beta-guaiacyl Ether (GBG) under optimal reaction conditions. The reaction product underwent three successive extractions using ethyl acetate and water. Then the extracts were combined and concentrated and sent to GC-MS for qualitative and relative quantitative analysis of the products. The method of GC-MS acid hydrolysis product analysis: the temperature program started at 45°C for 0 min, and the temperature was heated at 12°C to 300 °C/min and kept for 10 min.

### 3. Results and discussion #### 3.1. Analysis of DES pretreatment and content of SR components ##### 3.1.1. The effect of heating mode The LA-ChCl (LA:ChCl 10:1, molar ratio) was selected as the binary DES in this work based on our previous works (Liu et al., 2020; Cui et al., 2022).

As shown in Fig. 1, the delignification rate was greatly improved by stirring and microwave heating in the solvent system of LA-ChCl. The solvent can contact the raw materials more evenly and frequently by stirring, thus improving the treatment effect. Microwave improved the heating efficiency of the solvent, thus improving the treatment effect. Therefore, the combination of microwave and stirring was a relatively suitable pretreatment method. Fig. S1 shows the digital photos of SR obtained by different heating methods.

3.1.2. In this work, the function of the choline ion was remarkable. The delignification rate sustainably decreased when ChCl was replaced by NaCl. When ChCl was replaced by betaine, the delignification rate was the lowest, only 46.77%.

The previous report (Kanbayashi and Miyafuji, 2016) shows that ionic liquid based on the choline group can expand and rupture the cell wall, and the expansion of wood will increase its permeability. Consequently, the diffusion rate of LA into the cell wall will be accelerated, while the diffusion rate of lignin out of the cell wall will be enhanced, thus improving delignification efficiency. Our previous research (Liu et al., 2023, 2020) shows that choline ion directly participated in the reaction between solvent and lignin because N element and new hydrogen spectrum signals were detected in lignin obtained after treatment. Fig. S2 shows the digital photos of SR processed by DES with different HBA.

Carboxyl groups improved cleavage of lignin bonds because ethanol:ChCl 10:1 and isopropanol:ChCl 10:1 were not able to remove lignin at 140°C for one hour. The increase in alkyl chain length reduced the acidity and delignification rate of DESS (FA:ChCl 10:1 > AA:ChCl 10:1 > PA:ChCl 10:1).

Polyethylene glycol 400 (PEG 400), the third component, was introduced concerning the method of nitric acid ethanol, in which ethanol can protect cellulose from being degraded by nitric acid. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) is a good solubilizer and phase transfer catalyst. It has long hydrophobic alkyl chains and hydrophilic hydroxyl groups, and its properties are similar to lignin. It has been reported that long-chain diols can increase the dissolution of lignin and inhibit the condensation of lignin (Yu et al., 2022). In addition, PEG is a safe, non-toxic, and very stable solvent (usually considered a secure

compound) on the GRAS list of the FDA. It can be seen from Fig. 3 that the solid yield, the cellulose and hemicellulose recovery yield, and the delignification rate were all improved after adding PEG 400 at 140°C and 150°C for 1 h, and the cellulose recovery yield was almost 100%. This shows that the third component increased the dissolution of lignin while protecting cellulose and hemicellulose from degradation and further increased the deligni- fication selectivity of the DES. Analysis of simulated reactions by model compound The simulated reaction of the lignin model compound was carried out to better understand the reaction mechanism for lignin structural changes in the reaction system. The GC-MS analysis diagram of reaction products and the possible attribution of each peak in the diagram is shown in Fig. 13 and Tab. S5, respectively. The conversion rate of the lignin model compound was close to 100%, which indicates that the

reaction system in this study has high efficiency for lignin conversion and has the potential for future transformation and application of DES lignin. The possible reaction route for the lignin model compound to produce main products (integral area > 1%) is given (Fig. 14). The in- tegral area of PEG and LA was the biggest. Except for the signal of the solvent, guaiacol has the highest yield in monomer products, which supported the explanation for the increase of phenolic content in DESL. The appearance of G2 and G4 supports the description of the strong signal of DESL at 1736 cm⁻¹ in the previous FTIR analysis. The appearance of G5 indicated that LA may react with the phenolic hy- droxyl group of lignin. Combined with the emergence of new signal X in 2D-HSQC NMR analysis, it was speculated that signal X was G5.

In the whole reaction process, the aliphatic hydroxyl group in lignin and hydrogen proton in LA underwent a dehydration reaction, and the ̖-O-4 bond was cleaved to generate new monohydric phenol, which explained the reason why the aliphatic hydroxyl group decreased and the phenolic hydroxyl group increased in 21P NMR analysis. A small amount of monohydric phenol containing N element was found in the reaction product (30.61 min), which indicated that choline ions did participate in the bond-breaking reaction of lignin, and further confirmed that choline ions promoted the removal of lignin. In addition, a small amount of ferulic acid (28.84 min) and lignin ̖-5 condensation product (30.70 min) was detected in the product, which provided a possible explanation for the increase of carboxyl content in DES lignin in the 21P NMR analysis and the changes of ̖-5 content in lignin in 2D-HSQC NMR.

One reason is that in each cycle, the acidity of DES was reduced due to the bond breakage and dehydration reaction of lignin (Tab. S6). Another reason is that sugars produced by hydrolysis and part of lignin were dissolved in DES after each treatment, which significantly reduced the solubility of DES to lignin.

4. Conclusions This work developed a strategy for rapid microwave-assisted pre-treatment using a ternary deep eutectic solvent (LA:ChCl:PEG 400 (10:1+5%)) for lignin fractionation of eucalyptus. At atmospheric pressure and 140°C, the delignification rate was 89.73% in 30 min. The hydroxyl group in LA increased the polarity and proton-donating ability of the solution. Carboxyl groups provided hydrogen protons to break lignin bonds. The increase in alkyl chain length reduced the acidity of DES. Choline ion promoted the cleavage of the lignin β-O-4 bond. PEG 400 protected cellulose from degradation. Moreover, PEG 400, as a solubilizing agent, improved the solubility of DES for lignin, promoted the dissolution of lignin, and thus improved the delignification rate. DESL had low molecular weight, a small polydispersity index, and a relatively rich content of β-O-4 and phenolic hydroxyl groups, which has great application value and good application prospects. Monophenols and Hibbert ketone were the main products of the simulated reaction of lignin model compounds.

The test of Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs shows that the acidity and polarity of the solution greatly influence the delignification rate. The polyethylene glycol 400 increased the solubility of lignin in the solvent, improved the delignification rate, and protected cellulose from degradation. The gel permeation chromatography, 2D-HSQC NMR, and ³¹P NMR analysis show that the lignin obtained after DES treatment had low molecular weight, small polydispersity index, and relatively rich content of β-O-4 and phenolic hydroxyl groups, which has great application potential in high-value-added products from lignin. At the same time, the main products of the simulated reaction of the lignin model compound were monophenols and Hibbert ketone, and the possible reaction mechanism of changes in lignin during treatment was given. Our study lays a foundation for applying DES in biomass refining and the high-value utilization of lignin. # 1. Introduction The depletion of fossil fuels and pressing environmental concerns have engendered a significant inclination toward the pursuit of sustainable and renewable resources. Lignocellulosic biomass, characterized by its abundance and renewability, holds significant potential as a viable substitute for fossil-based feedstock. This biomass can be effectively transformed into both fuels and chemicals, offering a promising avenue for sustainable energy production and resource utilization (Liu et al., 2019; Rana et al., 2022, 2023; Rana, 2022). The primary constituents of lignocellulose are cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Lignin is the wealthiest resource of aromatic compounds in nature, and there are various applications for the utilization of this substance in the production of high-value fine chemicals, fuel products, and functional materials (Shen et al., 2019a). However, removing lignin from lignocellulosic biomass is difficult due to its complicated internal network structure and stubborn lignin. To overcome the inherent stubbornness of lignocellulose, researchers have developed different pretreatment methods to upgrade lignocellu- lose biomass into high-value products (Haghighi Mood et al., 2013). However, the strong corrosive nature of diluted acid, the high energy * Corresponding author. E-mail address: fesqhu@scut.edu.cn (S. Hu). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indcrop.2024.118297 Received 3 July 2023; Received in revised form 25 January 2024; Accepted 22 February 2024 Available online 1 March 2024 0926-6690/© 2024 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. and high-pressure requirements of steam explosion and hydrothermal pretreatment, the high volatility of organic solvents used in organic solvent pretreatment, and the high cost, toxicity, and poor biodegrad- ability of ionic liquids are some drawbacks that are typically associated with these techniques (Ci et al., 2020). Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), eutectic mixtures with a lower eutectic temperature than the ideal liquid combination, have recently received much interest in biomass pretreatment due to their remarkable selectivity for lignin removal (Tan et al., 2018; Alvarez-Vasco et al., 2016; da Costa Lopes et al., 2020). The DES system comprises a minimum of two hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) (Smith et al., 2014). Due to its cheap cost, non-toxicity, biodegradability, and economical production, the quaternary ammonium salt is the most extensively used HBA for DES, specifically choline chloride (ChCl) (Schutyser et al., 2018). ChCl-based DESs have been extensively utilized in diverse fields as an eco-friendly solvent alternative (Smith et al., 2014; Maugeri and de Maria, 2012; Zafarani-Moattar et al., 2016). However, the study of DES pretreatment usually focuses on non-wood (more than 80%) (Zhou et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2020; Wang and Lee, 2021). A more comprehensive investigation could be conducted regarding the availability of raw wood resources, Z. Liu et al. Industrial Crops & Products 212 (2024) 118297 especially focusing on eucalyptus, which is widely cultivated as hard-wood and exhibits a significant rate of production (Shen et al., 2019a). Compared with non-wood biomass materials, the dense structure of hardwood is more difficult to deconstruct. Therefore, it usually takes 6–12 h or more to get relatively satisfactory pretreatment results in the few studies on DES pretreatment of eucalyptus (Hong et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2019b; Chen et al., 2021; Soares et al., 2021). Long pretreatment time and the acidity of DES will lead to lignin condensation and reduce the efficiency of enzyme treatment (Hong et al., 2020a). In addition, long-term pretreatment will lead to various side effects and degradation of DES and cellulose (Morais et al., 2021). Hence, it is imperative to expeditiously execute the delignification process to segregate biomass into superior-grade cellulose fibers and lignin. Microwave pretreatment has been widely employed in many bio-refining processes due to its non-contact heat source, low residence time, and minimal adverse ef-fects (Zhong et al., 2022; Muley et al., 2019). Furthermore, microwave radiation has been demonstrated to improve the ionic properties of DES and raise the molecular polarity (Chen and Wan, 2018). Microwave-assisted deep eutectic solvents (DES) have been proven effective for delignification of non-wood biomass feedstocks. For instance, Yan et al. (2023) treated rice straw continuously for 4 min under microwave irradiation (680 W) at a 1:30 solid to liquid ratio using a ternary DES (choline chloride: oxalic acid: lactic acid 1:0.5:1, molar ratio), yielding a 63.4% lignin removal rate. Chourasia et al (Chourasia et al., 2022). employed a choline chloride/ethylene glycol/NiCl2·6H2O system (molar ratio 1:2:0.016 with 20 wt% water as co-solvent) to treat sugarcane bagasse at 100°C for 30 min at 10% solid loading, reaching 84% delignification. Ji et al (Ji et al., 2020). utilized a ternary DES (ChCl-Gly-Al at molar ratio 1:2:0.2) under consecutive ultrasound (20 + 28 + 40 kHz, room temperature, 30 min) and microwave (80°C, 20 min) treatment of garlic skin to attain 90.14% lignin removal. Hence, it is plausible that the utilization of microwaves can reduce the duration of the reaction process in DES pretreatment of eucalyptus compared with DES pretreatment alone and achieve similar or even higher efficiency. This study has devised an eco-friendly, gentle, and effective tech- nique for pretreatment by utilizing a ternary deep eutectic solvent to fractionate lignin from eucalyptus. Materials Samples of Eucalyptus were obtained from a commercial forest farm in Paiyang Mountain, China. The composition of the Eucalyptus was determined to be 25.68% lignin, 46.40% cellulose, and 27.92% hemi-cellulose, based on the dried extracted raw materials. The specific experimental procedures and relevant formulas could be found in the supply materials (Note. S2). Eucalyptus wood powder passing through 40 mesh sieves was selected as the raw material (RM). The milled wood lignin (MWL) and alkali lignin (AL) were obtained based on the reported routes (Wen et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023). The support information could include specific steps (Note. S1). The reagents used in this work are analytically pure and purchased from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd. ## 2.2. Methods ### 2.2.1. Preparation of DESs Several commonly used DESs for biomass pretreatments were prepared. Specific components and proportions can be found in Tab. S1. Specifically, a beaker was filled with a specified molar ratio of HBAs and HBDs. The obtained DESs were then kept at room temperature after being agitated in a water bath at 60°C to produce a clear solvent. ### 2.2.2. DES pretreatment and DES recycling The pretreatment process was conducted utilizing a conical flask, wherein the biomass concentration was maintained at 10 wt% (5.00 g of dry biomass and 50.00 g of reagents). The pretreatment was carried out under different target conditions (solvent type, heating mode, time, etc.) The resulting liquid and solid were transferred to a 500 mL beaker containing 250 mL of washing solvent (acetone: ethanol 1:1 v:v) and agitated for 6 h after pretreatment. Following that, the combined solution was filtered through a G2 glass filter, and the solid residue (SR) was washed with washing solvent until the filtrate was colorless. Rotary evaporation was used to concentrate the filtrate, which was subsequently placed into water to precipitate lignin. The SR and lignin obtained from the DES pretreatment (DESL) were dried in a vacuum oven at 40°C. By evaporating the liquid, DES was recovered and reused. 2.2.3. Component analysis of SR The lignin content in SR was determined by the two-step acid hy- drolysis (Shen et al., 2019b), the cellulose content in SR was determined by the nitric acid-alcohol method, and hemicellulose content was calculated by subtraction. The specific experimental procedures and relevant formulas could be found in the supply materials (Note. S2). 2.2.4. Measurement of the Kamlet–Taft (K-T) solvatochromic parameters of DESs The K-T solvatochromic parameters of DESs used in this work were measured based on reported routes (Dwamena and Raynie, 2020), where α stands for hydrogen bond acidity, the β stands for hydrogen bond alkalinity, and the π* stands for the polarity of the solvent. The specific steps and relevant formulas can be found in the support information (Note. S3). 2.2.5. Characterizations of lignin The application of gel permeation chromatography (GPC) was employed to assess the acetylation of materials for the purpose of determining the distribution of molecular weight (Mw) in lignin. The chemical structures of lignin were studied using Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy and 2D-HSQC NMR. The 31P NMR spectra were used to measure the phenolic hydroxyl, alcohol hydroxyl, and carboxyl concentrations of lignin. Conclusions This work developed a strategy for rapid microwave-assisted pre-treatment using a ternary deep eutectic solvent (LA:ChCl:PEG 400 (10:1+5%)) for lignin fractionation of eucalyptus. At atmospheric pressure and 140°C, the delignification rate was 89.73% in 30 min. The hydroxyl group in LA increased the polarity and proton-donating ability of the solution. Carboxyl groups provided hydrogen protons to break lignin bonds. The increase in alkyl chain length reduced the acidity of DES. Choline ion promoted the cleavage of the lignin β-O-4 bond. PEG 400 protected cellulose from degradation. Moreover, PEG 400, as a solubilizing agent, improved the solubility of DES for lignin, promoted the dissolution of lignin, and thus improved the delignification rate. DESL had low molecular weight, a small polydispersity index, and a relatively rich content of β-O-4 and phenolic hydroxyl groups, which has great application value and good application prospects. Monophenols and Hibbert ketone were the main products of the simulated reaction of lignin model compounds. The test of Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs shows that the acidity and polarity of the solution greatly influence the delignification rate. The polyethylene glycol 400 increased the solubility of lignin in the solvent, improved the delignification rate, and protected cellulose from degradation. The gel permeation chromatography, 2D-HSQC NMR, and ³¹P NMR analysis show that the lignin obtained after DES treatment had low molecular weight, small polydispersity index, and relatively rich content of β-O-4 and phenolic hydroxyl groups, which has great application potential in high-value-added products from lignin. At the same time, the main products of the simulated reaction of the lignin model compound were monophenols and Hibbert ketone, and the possible reaction mechanism of changes in lignin during treatment was given. Our study lays a foundation for applying DES in biomass refining and the high-value utilization of lignin. # 1. Introduction The depletion of fossil fuels and pressing environmental concerns have engendered a significant inclination toward the pursuit of sustainable and renewable resources. Lignocellulosic biomass, characterized by its abundance and renewability, holds significant potential as a viable substitute for fossil-based feedstock. This biomass can be effectively transformed into both fuels and chemicals, offering a promising avenue for sustainable energy production and resource utilization (Liu et al., 2019; Rana et al., 2022, 2023; Rana, 2022). The primary constituents of lignocellulose are cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin. Lignin is the wealthiest resource of aromatic compounds in nature, and there are various applications for the utilization of this substance in the production of high-value fine chemicals, fuel products, and functional materials (Shen et al., 2019a). However, removing lignin from lignocellulosic biomass is difficult due to its complicated internal network structure and stubborn lignin. To overcome the inherent stubbornness of lignocellulose, researchers have developed different pretreatment methods to upgrade lignocellu- lose biomass into high-value products (Haghighi Mood et al., 2013). However, the strong corrosive nature of diluted acid, the high energy * Corresponding author. E-mail address: fesqhu@scut.edu.cn (S. All rights reserved. and high-pressure requirements of steam explosion and hydrothermal pretreatment, the high volatility of organic solvents used in organic solvent pretreatment, and the high cost, toxicity, and poor biodegrad- ability of ionic liquids are some drawbacks that are typically associated with these techniques (Ci et al., 2020). Deep eutectic solvents (DESs), eutectic mixtures with a lower eutectic temperature than the ideal liquid combination, have recently received much interest in biomass pretreatment due to their remarkable selectivity for lignin removal (Tan et al., 2018; Alvarez-Vasco et al., 2016; da Costa Lopes et al., 2020). The DES system comprises a minimum of two hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) (Smith et al., 2014). Due to its cheap cost, non-toxicity, biodegradability, and economical production, the quaternary ammonium salt is the most extensively used HBA for DES, specifically choline chloride (ChCl) (Schutyser et al., 2018). ChCl-based DESs have been extensively utilized in diverse fields as an eco-friendly solvent alternative (Smith et al., 2014; Maugeri and de Maria, 2012; Zafarani-Moattar et al., 2016). However, the study of DES pretreatment usually focuses on non-wood (more than 80%) (Zhou et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2020; Wang and Lee, 2021). A more comprehensive investigation could be conducted regarding the availability of raw wood resources, Z. Liu et al. Industrial Crops & Products 212 (2024) 118297 especially focusing on eucalyptus, which is widely cultivated as hard-wood and exhibits a significant rate of production (Shen et al., 2019a). Compared with non-wood biomass materials, the dense structure of hardwood is more difficult to deconstruct. Therefore, it usually takes 6–12 h or more to get relatively satisfactory pretreatment results in the few studies on DES pretreatment of eucalyptus (Hong et al., 2022; Shen et al., 2019b; Chen et al., 2021; Soares et al., 2021). Long pretreatment time and the acidity of DES will lead to lignin condensation and reduce the efficiency of enzyme treatment (Hong et al., 2020a). In addition, long-term pretreatment will lead to various side effects and degradation of DES and cellulose (Morais et al., 2021). Hence, it is imperative to expeditiously execute the delignification process to segregate biomass into superior-grade cellulose fibers and lignin. Microwave pretreatment has been widely employed in many bio-refining processes due to its non-contact heat source, low residence time, and minimal adverse ef-fects (Zhong et al., 2022; Muley et al., 2019). Furthermore, microwave radiation has been demonstrated to improve the ionic properties of DES and raise the molecular polarity (Chen and Wan, 2018). Microwave-assisted deep eutectic solvents (DES) have been proven effective for delignification of non-wood biomass feedstocks. For instance, Yan et al. (2023) treated rice straw continuously for 4 min under microwave irradiation (680 W) at a 1:30 solid to liquid ratio using a ternary DES (choline chloride: oxalic acid: lactic acid 1:0.5:1, molar ratio), yielding a 63.4% lignin removal rate. Chourasia et al (Chourasia et al., 2022). employed a choline chloride/ethylene glycol/NiCl2·6H2O system (molar ratio 1:2:0.016 with 20 wt% water as co-solvent) to treat sugarcane bagasse at 100°C for 30 min at 10% solid loading, reaching 84% delignification. Ji et al (Ji et al., 2020). utilized a ternary DES (ChCl-Gly-Al at molar ratio 1:2:0.2) under consecutive ultrasound (20 + 28 + 40 kHz, room temperature, 30 min) and microwave (80°C, 20 min) treatment of garlic skin to attain 90.14% lignin removal. Hence, it is plausible that the utilization of microwaves can reduce the duration of the reaction process in DES pretreatment of eucalyptus compared with DES pretreatment alone and achieve similar or even higher efficiency. This study has devised an eco-friendly, gentle, and effective tech- nique for pretreatment by utilizing a ternary deep eutectic solvent to fractionate lignin from eucalyptus. Materials Samples of Eucalyptus were obtained from a commercial forest farm in Paiyang Mountain, China. The composition of the Eucalyptus was determined to be 25.68% lignin, 46.40% cellulose, and 27.92% hemi-cellulose, based on the dried extracted raw materials. The specific experimental procedures and relevant formulas could be found in the supply materials (Note. S2). Eucalyptus wood powder passing through 40 mesh sieves was selected as the raw material (RM). The milled wood lignin (MWL) and alkali lignin (AL) were obtained based on the reported routes (Wen et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023). The support information could include specific steps (Note. S1). The reagents used in this work are analytically pure and purchased from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd. ## 2.2. Methods ### 2.2.1. Preparation of DESs Several commonly used DESs for biomass pretreatments were prepared. Specific components and proportions can be found in Tab. S1. Specifically, a beaker was filled with a specified molar ratio of HBAs and HBDs. The obtained DESs were then kept at room temperature after being agitated in a water bath at 60°C to produce a clear solvent. ### 2.2.2. DES pretreatment and DES recycling The pretreatment process was conducted utilizing a conical flask, wherein the biomass concentration was maintained at 10 wt% (5.00 g of dry biomass and 50.00 g of reagents). The pretreatment was carried out under different target conditions (solvent type, heating mode, time, etc.) The resulting liquid and solid were transferred to a 500 mL beaker containing 250 mL of washing solvent (acetone: ethanol 1:1 v:v) and agitated for 6 h after pretreatment. Following that, the combined solution was filtered through a G2 glass filter, and the solid residue (SR) was washed with washing solvent until the filtrate was colorless. Rotary evaporation was used to concentrate the filtrate, which was subsequently placed into water to precipitate lignin. The SR and lignin obtained from the DES pretreatment (DESL) were dried in a vacuum oven at 40°C. By evaporating the liquid, DES was recovered and reused. 2.2.3. Component analysis of SR The lignin content in SR was determined by the two-step acid hy- drolysis (Shen et al., 2019b), the cellulose content in SR was determined by the nitric acid-alcohol method, and hemicellulose content was calculated by subtraction. The specific experimental procedures and relevant formulas could be found in the supply materials (Note. S2). 2.2.4. Measurement of the Kamlet–Taft (K-T) solvatochromic parameters of DESs The K-T solvatochromic parameters of DESs used in this work were measured based on reported routes (Dwamena and Raynie, 2020), where α stands for hydrogen bond acidity, the β stands for hydrogen bond alkalinity, and the π* stands for the polarity of the solvent. Conclusions This work developed a strategy for rapid microwave-assisted pre-treatment using a ternary deep eutectic solvent (LA:ChCl:PEG 400 (10:1+5%)) for lignin fractionation of eucalyptus. At atmospheric pressure and 140°C, the delignification rate was 89.73% in 30 min. The hydroxyl group in LA increased the polarity and proton-donating ability of the solution. Carboxyl groups provided hydrogen protons to break lignin bonds. The increase in alkyl chain length reduced the acidity of DES. Choline ion promoted the cleavage of the lignin β-O-4 bond. PEG 400 protected cellulose from degradation. Moreover, PEG 400, as a solubilizing agent, improved the solubility of DES for lignin, promoted the dissolution of lignin, and thus improved the delignification rate. DESL had low molecular weight, a small polydispersity index, and a relatively rich content of β-O-4 and phenolic hydroxyl groups, which has great application value and good application prospects. Monophenols and Hibbert ketone were the main products of the simulated reaction of lignin model compounds.
